quote: Even the hairs of your head have all been counted.
firstReading: Ephesians proclaims that believers have received an inheritance in Christ according to the purpose of God, who accomplishes all things according to his will. Those who first hoped in Christ exist for the praise of his glory. Having heard the word of truth, the Gospel of salvation, and believed, they were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the pledge of the final redemption of God’s people.
psalmSummary: Psalm 33 summons the righteous to praise the Lord with joyful worship because his word is upright and all his works are trustworthy. He loves justice and right, and the earth is filled with his kindness. Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people chosen as his inheritance. From heaven, the Lord looks upon every human being with attentive knowledge and sovereign care.
gospelSummary: As crowds gather around Jesus, he first warns his disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees, identifying it as hypocrisy. What is hidden will be revealed, so disciples must not shape their lives by concealment or fear. Jesus teaches them not to fear those who can kill the body but have no further power; rather, they must reverence God, whose judgment is final. Yet this holy fear is inseparable from confidence in the Father’s care. Sparrows, though of little earthly value, are not forgotten by God, and every hair on the disciples’ heads is counted. Therefore, Jesus commands them not to be afraid: they are worth far more than many sparrows.
saintReflection: Saint Hedwig and Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque (Optional Memorials): Saint Hedwig of Silesia (c. 1174–1243) and Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque (1647–1690) are honored through optional memorials. Hedwig lived marriage, motherhood, widowhood, and religious devotion with sustained care for people in poverty, prisoners, and the sick, while supporting monastic life and reconciliation. Margaret Mary, a Visitation nun, promoted devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus after spiritual experiences tested within her community and the Church. That devotion contemplates the incarnate love of Christ, especially his self-giving in the Paschal Mystery and the Eucharist, and calls for reparation, trust, and renewed charity. Together these saints show that love of Christ takes both contemplative and practical form. Their witness invites perseverance through misunderstanding, tenderness toward suffering, sacramental devotion, and a heart conformed to the merciful love revealed in Jesus.
dailyPrayer:
Father of mercies, you chose us in Christ and sealed us with the Holy Spirit as the pledge of our inheritance. Purify us from hypocrisy, from the divided heart that seeks to appear faithful while withholding itself from your truth. Grant us the holy fear that worships you alone and the filial confidence that rests in your providence. You know us more deeply than we know ourselves, and no suffering, hidden prayer, or act of mercy escapes your loving gaze.

Through the intercession of Saint Hedwig, make us attentive to people in poverty, prisoners, the sick, and all who bear sorrow. Through Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque, draw us to the Sacred Heart of your Son, especially in the Eucharist. Teach us to receive his self-giving love, to offer reparation for sin, and to answer injury with patient charity. May the Holy Spirit conform our hearts to Jesus, so that our words and deeds may praise your glory. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings unite election, truthful discipleship, and divine providence. Ephesians teaches that God’s saving purpose is realized in Christ and received through faith, with the Holy Spirit sealing believers for the redemption still to come. Christian hope therefore rests not on human concealment or control, but on God’s faithful action. Psalm 33 answers this grace with praise: the Lord’s word is upright, his works are dependable, and his gaze embraces those he has made.

In Luke, Jesus exposes hypocrisy because disciples belong wholly to the God who sees all things. Fear of human opposition cannot govern those whose final destiny lies in God’s hands. The Lord’s warning about judgment is not meant to estrange the faithful from the Father; it forms reverence within the assurance that God forgets none of his creatures. Saints Hedwig and Margaret Mary embody this truth through mercy toward the suffering, perseverance amid trial, Eucharistic devotion, reparation, and trust in Christ’s merciful Heart. The Spirit seals the Church for a love that is both adoring and active.
exegesis:
Context: Ephesians 1 stands within the apostle’s great blessing of God for the saving work accomplished in Christ. The passage speaks first of those who hoped in Christ and then of the readers who heard the word of truth and believed. The emphasis is not on a private religious possession but on God’s gracious purpose: believers have been claimed for an inheritance and are themselves God’s people. This election reaches its proper end in praise of God’s glory. The Church’s identity begins in the Father’s saving will, is centered on the Son, and is brought to completion by the Holy Spirit.

Context: The Spirit is described as the seal and pledge of the promised inheritance. A seal marks belonging and authenticity; the pledge indicates that the final redemption is truly promised though not yet fully manifested. Thus baptismal faith introduces Christians into a real participation in salvation while directing them toward its fulfillment. The reading does not invite presumption. It summons the baptized to live as a people whose lives proclaim God’s glory, trusting the Spirit who preserves and sanctifies them until the day of complete redemption.

Psalm: Psalm 33 supplies the worshipful response to this saving purpose. God’s word is right, and his deeds are faithful; justice and right are not abstractions but qualities of the Lord’s own action. The psalm also calls blessed the people whose God is the Lord, language that harmonizes with Ephesians’ account of a people received as God’s inheritance. Divine choosing is therefore ordered toward communion, praise, and fidelity. The Lord who sees from heaven is neither distant nor indifferent. His universal knowledge establishes confidence that human lives are held beneath his wise and just gaze.

Gospel: Luke situates Jesus before an immense crowd, but his first instruction is addressed to his disciples. He warns them against the leaven of the Pharisees, which he names hypocrisy. Leaven works quietly through dough; so hypocrisy can penetrate religious life when outward appearance is separated from truth before God. Jesus declares that hidden things will be uncovered. This is both warning and liberation. What disciples say and do need not be governed by anxiety about preserving an image, because the God who judges sees the heart already. Truthfulness before him is the proper foundation of witness.

Gospel: Jesus then distinguishes fear of persecutors from reverence for God. Human beings may inflict bodily death, a grave reality that Christ does not minimize. Yet they cannot determine the disciple’s ultimate destiny. God alone possesses authority over final judgment, and therefore he alone must be feared in the biblical sense of awe, obedience, and worship. Immediately Jesus joins this warning to a tender proclamation of providence. Sparrows are not forgotten, and the disciples are known with a care extending even to the hairs of their heads. Holy fear and filial trust belong together: the Judge is also the Father whose knowledge of his children is loving and particular.

Saints: Saint Hedwig of Silesia gives practical expression to a life placed beneath God’s gaze. Her sustained care for people in poverty, prisoners, and the sick, together with her support for monastic life and reconciliation, shows that faith in God’s mercy bears fruit in concrete mercy. Her life across marriage, motherhood, widowhood, and religious devotion witnesses that every state of life can be received as an occasion for faithful charity. Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque’s promotion of devotion to the Sacred Heart directs the Church to the incarnate love of Christ, above all in his Paschal self-giving and in the Eucharist. The testing of her spiritual experiences within her community and the Church also recalls that devotion is discerned ecclesially, not isolated from the Church’s judgment.

Saints: Together, Hedwig and Margaret Mary illuminate the readings’ movement from divine election to a transformed heart and merciful action. Devotion to the Sacred Heart calls the faithful to reparation, trust, and charity because Christ’s heart reveals the depth of his redemptive love. Care for the suffering makes visible the same love received in contemplation and sacrament. Neither saint’s witness permits a division between worship and mercy. The Spirit promised in Ephesians forms believers to adore Christ truly and to serve him in those who endure need, illness, imprisonment, or misunderstanding.

Today: The Church is called to reject every form of hypocrisy, especially any separation between prayer, sacramental devotion, and charity toward the vulnerable. Christians need not live under the tyranny of human approval, for their worth is established by the Father who knows and remembers them. At the same time, confidence in divine care must not dull reverence before God’s judgment. It should purify the heart, strengthen perseverance, and lead to truthfulness. Sealed by the Holy Spirit, the faithful can entrust themselves to Christ’s merciful love, praise the Father’s glory, and carry that love into acts of reconciliation, tenderness, and faithful service.
